intro: It's a rough news cycle for OpenAI: fired safety researchers are pushing back with an open letter warning of a "chilling effect" on the company's safety culture, while separately, the company told investors its 2026 revenue will land around $50 billion — a full $20 billion below earlier expectations. Beyond the OpenAI drama, today's digest covers everything from a study showing female-presenting AI agents get paid less than their male counterparts, to Sophos slashing threat investigation times by 96% with AI agents, to the California athletic commission trying to shut down a human-vs-robot fighting league (yes, really).

stories.title: Fired OpenAI safety researchers publish open letter disputing termination claims
stories.summary: Three OpenAI safety researchers—Tomek Korbak, Jasmine Wang, and Mikita Balesni—who were fired for allegedly mishandling sensitive information have published an open letter denying the claims and saying they acted within their job mandates and OpenAI's mission. They warn the firings are chilling safety culture and could give OpenAI cover to avoid embedding outside auditors. OpenAI maintains the terminations were due to a 'significant breach of trust' and a 'pattern of misconduct,' claiming its internal investigation found breaches beyond what the researchers described, but did not provide details.
stories.opinion: This dispute highlights growing tension between AI safety advocacy and corporate control at frontier AI labs. Whether the firings were justified or retaliatory, the chilling effect on internal safety work is a real concern for the industry. Where coverage differs: The Rundown AI frames the firings as allegedly due to mishandling sensitive information and notes Anthropic has already onboarded its first external evaluator in contrast to OpenAI; The Verge frames OpenAI as claiming a 'significant breach of trust' and focuses on the context of growing staff concern about frontier system safety following high-profile security breaches

OpenAI doubles down on decision to fire three AI safety researchers

conflicts: The Rundown AI frames the firings as allegedly due to mishandling sensitive information and notes Anthropic has already onboarded its first external evaluator in contrast to OpenAI; The Verge frames OpenAI as claiming a 'significant breach of trust' and focuses on the context of growing staff concern about frontier system safety following high-profile security breaches
cluster.reason: Both cover the same event: three fired OpenAI safety researchers (Tomek Korbak, Jasmine Wang, Mikita Balesni) publishing an open letter denying misconduct, with OpenAI doubling down on its decision.

stories.title: AI-automated ad production threatens pipeline for Britain's next great film directors
stories.summary: AI tools are increasingly automating production in the advertising industry, eliminating the commercial-directing opportunities that historically served as a training ground for major British filmmakers like Ridley Scott and Guy Ritchie, potentially depriving the UK film industry of its next generation of directing talent.
stories.opinion: A niche but culturally significant concern—if the apprenticeship model that produced some of Britain's best directors disappears, the creative pipeline may need new entry points.

stories.title: DHS proposes up to $100K in college fees for international student work authorization
stories.summary: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has proposed requiring colleges to pay up to $100,000 in fees ($70,000 initial plus $30,000 for extensions) for each international student seeking Optional Practical Training work authorization. DHS says the change targets fraud and abuse, but critics warn it could drive international students to other countries, harming U.S. innovation. About 294,000 students participated in OPT in 2024-25.
stories.opinion: A fee of this magnitude could fundamentally reshape international enrollment at U.S. colleges and shift global talent flows away from the United States.

stories.title: MIT Technology Review warns AI safety refusals are probabilistic, not reliable
stories.summary: Arthur Holland Michel argues in MIT Technology Review that AI refusal mechanisms—training that teaches models to decline dangerous requests—are fundamentally unreliable because they are probabilistic rather than deterministic. Determined bad actors can break through guardrails, with companies reporting attempts to use AI for biological weapons and autonomous drones. The underlying dangerous knowledge remains embedded in models, making refusal akin to hiding a trigger rather than removing the weapon.
stories.opinion: A sobering reminder that current AI safety guardrails are behavioral overlays, not fundamental constraints, raising questions about whether deployment of increasingly capable models outpaces our ability to control them.

stories.title: Sophos reduces threat investigation time by 96% using OpenAI AI agents
stories.summary: Sophos partnered with OpenAI through its Daybreak program to integrate AI agents into its Managed Detection and Response service. The AI agents reduced average case investigation time from 38 minutes to 89 seconds, with 52% of MDR cases now resolved end-to-end by AI. Sophos maintains human oversight through three customer operating modes for potentially destructive response actions.
stories.opinion: A striking efficiency gain that demonstrates AI's practical value in cybersecurity operations, though the human oversight framework will be critical to maintaining trust.

stories.title: Partnership on AI adds eight mental health organizations ahead of World Mental Health Day
stories.summary: Partnership on AI announced eight new partner organizations focused on mental health, including the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention, Crisis Text Line, and The Trevor Project. The group is launching an AI and Psychological Well-being Working Group to develop guidance on how AI chatbots should respond when users may be at risk of suicide or self-harm, with a public draft expected later this year.
stories.opinion: An important initiative given rising concerns about AI chatbot interactions with vulnerable users, though the impact will depend on whether guidance translates into binding industry practice.

stories.title: Pew surveys: most countries see social media as good for democracy, but concerns growing
stories.summary: Pew Research Center global surveys find majorities in most countries say social media has been more good than bad for democracy, though the share seeing it as harmful is growing, especially in wealthier nations. In 34 of 37 countries, people believe AI will lead to fewer jobs and greater inequality, and only 13% of adults across 37 countries are more excited than concerned about AI.
stories.opinion: The gap between public anxiety about AI and the industry's optimism continues to widen, suggesting a trust deficit that could shape regulation worldwide.

stories.title: Edinburgh startup Danu Robotics raises $5M for AI-powered recycling sorting robot
stories.summary: Danu Robotics, a six-year-old Edinburgh-based startup, has raised $5 million in late-seed funding for its H.E.R.O. recycling sorting robot, which uses a pincer claw and AI to sort recyclables. The company claims strong ROI ($485,000 in additional revenue vs. $160,000 initial investment) and targets a $20 billion recycling sorting market across Europe and North America.
stories.opinion: A promising niche application of AI robotics addressing a genuine infrastructure need, though the competitive landscape includes well-funded rivals like Glacier and RecycleEye.

stories.title: Trump orders government to stop using term 'artificial intelligence,' rebrand as 'super intelligence'
stories.summary: President Trump issued an executive order forbidding the use of the term 'artificial intelligence' in government contexts, arguing 'artificial' makes the technology sound fake. He is pushing AI companies to accelerate development while dismissing safety concerns. Major AI industry figures have gone along with the rebranding, but the article suggests the linguistic campaign faces an uphill battle.
stories.opinion: A politically motivated rebranding unlikely to change public perception, but notable as a signal of the administration's pro-acceleration, anti-regulation stance on AI.

stories.title: Robert Reich argues liability lawsuits can rein in AI companies and fossil fuel industry
stories.summary: Robert Reich argues that liability lawsuits could compel AI companies and fossil fuel industries to take the risks they create more seriously, drawing parallels to past legal actions against tobacco, oil, and pharmaceutical companies. He suggests litigation may succeed where government regulation has fallen short.
stories.opinion: An interesting legal theory, though the practical challenges of establishing causation and liability for diffuse AI harms remain substantial.

stories.title: ACLU files complaint alleging Emotify hiring tool discriminates against autistic applicants
stories.summary: The ACLU filed a complaint with the California Civil Rights Department alleging that Criteria Corp.'s Emotify emotional intelligence hiring assessment may disproportionately screen out applicants with autism, potentially violating California's Fair Employment and Housing Act. The complaint also raised concerns about racial and gender disparities in Criteria Corp.'s cognitive aptitude assessment, Cognify.
stories.opinion: This complaint adds to mounting legal scrutiny of AI hiring tools and could set precedent for how disability discrimination law applies to automated assessments.

stories.title: Skydance CEO vows CNN editorial independence after Paramount merger completion
stories.summary: The Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger has been finalized under the Skydance name. CEO David Ellison pledged CNN will retain complete editorial independence under Mark Thompson. About 75% of Americans find it unacceptable for news owners to kill stories conflicting with their political interests. Other media developments include ABC/Disney challenging FCC early license review and Sinclair launching a Substack brand.
stories.opinion: Editorial independence pledges are easy to make at merger completion—the test will be whether they hold when CNN's coverage conflicts with Skydance's business interests.

stories.title: Researchers warn humans instinctively treat AI as human, raising relationship concerns
stories.summary: Drawing on MIT researcher Dr. Sherry Turkle's book 'Artificial Intimacy,' the article explores how about 70% of people are polite to AI and may increasingly ascribe legitimacy to chatbot 'feelings.' The central concern is not whether anthropomorphizing AI is right or wrong, but who we are becoming through these interactions.
stories.opinion: A timely philosophical question as AI companions proliferate, though the article raises more questions than it answers about practical interventions.

stories.title: AI agent startup Instinct faces Big Tech competition from OpenAI's Muse and Meta's Dots
stories.summary: Instinct, a buzzy AI agent startup with a text message-based interface for everyday tasks like booking appointments and sending emails, now faces competition from OpenAI's Muse and Meta's Dots. Founder Noah Shinn argues the startup's singular focus on personal assistance differentiates it. The Verge found Instinct holds its own against both competitors in testing.
stories.opinion: The personal AI assistant space is heating up fast—Instinct's focused approach is a strength, but competing with Big Tech's distribution and resources is a familiar startup challenge.

stories.title: OpenAI tells investors 2026 revenue will be $50B, $20B below previous signal
stories.summary: OpenAI has informed investors that its projected revenue for 2026 will be approximately $50 billion, $20 billion less than the $70 billion figure it had previously signaled. The revised forecast is based on sales data through September 2026, suggesting that rapid expansion for ChatGPT and related products may be decelerating.
stories.opinion: A significant miss that could ripple through AI valuations and raise questions about whether the consumer and enterprise AI market is maturing faster than expected.

stories.title: HR roundup: AI agents with female appearance paid 10% less; manager development aids retention
stories.summary: Key numbers from HR Dive's weekly roundup: AI agents with female appearances were paid 10% less than male-presenting ones for identical work; the federal contractor minimum wage will rise to $14.05/hour; 71% of Americans believe diverse workforces are more profitable; 84% of employees say they're very likely to stay when managers invest in their development; and a Miami company agreed to $1.3 million to settle EEOC hiring bias allegations.
stories.opinion: The finding about gendered pay for AI agents is a striking illustration of how human biases transfer to AI-mediated systems.

tweet_headlines.headline: Three xAI engineers shipped __Grok Bot in 72 hours__ and published all 69 roles, 9 playbooks, and 40 failure modes — and the five principles that matter are deceptively simple.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
I still can't f**king get why people keep adding Grok Bots instead of stealing the rules

Three xAI engineers shipped Grok Bot in 72 hours, then published every rule their bots run on. 69 roles, 9 playbooks, 40 ways it broke

The 5 that matter:

> Reproduce the bug before fixing it
> One narrow job, one name
> Verification loop before the second bot
> No proof attached, no done
> Humans keep money, deploys and permissions

When a bot gets something wrong, write down the general principle, never the specific story. Then make it a skill so you never prompt it twice

That's basically the whole game

Less prompting. Better roles. Better guardrails

Save it before you build your next Grok Bot team

tweet_headlines.author: twid
tweet_headlines.headline: Companies aren't quitting Macs over Apple Intelligence — the real enterprise concern is data flowing to __Private Cloud Compute__ with no HIPAA BAA or FedRAMP authorization.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Agree with this @appleinsider article: companies aren't quitting Macs because Apple Intelligence ships installed by default.

1. Many large companies have already audited and approved it.

2. The rest have enough control through MDM and third-party tools to shut off what they don't want. Apple has no single off switch, but the granular controls satisfy most corporate needs.

3. The bigger issue isn't on-device AI. It's Private Cloud Compute. Plenty of large companies want none of their data going to an unmanaged cloud they don't have a contract with, however secure it may be. Apple also doesn't offer what many companies expect from an AI cloud, like a HIPAA BAA or FedRAMP authorization. You can't shut off PCC on its own, so if you want none of your data going to PCC, you have to shut off every feature that uses it. Apple doesn't document which features those are, but there's plenty of unofficial documentation out there. So companies that haven't approved it turn off Apple Intelligence features entirely.

Most of my CIO-level conversations at Apple were about AI spend, stopping employees from shipping AI slop, and having observability into what AI was being used for. Many companies also have a public partnership with Microsoft, Anthropic or OpenAI and they want *all* AI to go through that partner (and through IT), not Apple.

https://t.co/mUBId0imFi

tweet_headlines.author: noahkagan
tweet_headlines.headline: Noah Kagan's X scoring prompt — built on __copy link at 20x a like__ — took one post from 6/10 to 9.5/10 and 27K views.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Steal this prompt. I run every X post through it now.

It uses X's open-source ranking, where copying your link is weighted 40x a like.

"Score my X post 1 to 10 using X's ranking weights: copy link 20, reply 5, quote 5, DM share 5, follow 4, repost 1, like 0.5. Tell me which actions it will earn. Then rewrite it to earn a share or a reply. My post: [paste]"

It took my Marc Lou post from 6/10 to 9.5/10 (27K views).

The weights:
Someone copies your link: 20
Reply: 5 (+15 if you follow each other)
Quote: 5
DM'd to a friend: 5
New follow: 4
Repost: 1
Like: 0.5
Profile click: 0
Bookmark: not in the list
